prompt:
Create a finished illustration for a public book-summary library for adult readers. Use a calm, contemporary illustrated-book style: hand-painted gouache, soft matte pigment, restrained pencil details, and a subtle warm ivory paper texture. Use a consistent palette of muted sage and olive green, warm ochre, natural wood brown, and warm ivory, with dark brown or charcoal details. Keep saturation restrained and lighting soft and natural. Give the scene generous breathing room, a clear focal point, and simple, recognizable forms that remain readable on a phone. When people are relevant, depict believable adults with natural proportions, respectful expressions, and ordinary clothing. Use the same medium, palette, texture, and level of detail across the illustration. Avoid photorealism, glossy 3D, neon colors, cinematic effects, heavy black outlines, childish clipart, ornamental clutter, and a different art style in each panel. No readable text, captions, logos, watermarks, fake book covers, or invented author portraits. Keep all explanations and essential labels outside the generated image.

Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: finished SQUARE hero illustration for a
book-summary article. The supplied reference is a STYLE REFERENCE ONLY. Match its
gouache, paper texture, matte pigments and gentle natural light. Do not copy its
person, study desk, notebook or scene. Use a NEW concrete subject and composition
appropriate to the book below. Choose a clear single scene or visual metaphor that
conveys the central idea, using the summary as context. Do not render the title,
author name, quotations, text, labels, equations or a book cover. No random abstract
shards, generic tech networks, diagram labels, glossy objects or flat-vector icons.
Avoid a person at a study desk as a default. Use people only when they help explain
this particular subject. For biographies, evoke the person's work, historical
setting or defining subject through places and objects, without inventing an author
or historical person's likeness. Do not depict a speculative documentary event.
For novels, choose an appropriate setting, object or restrained symbolic scene;
preserve the work's tone without graphic violence, sexual imagery or fake covers.
For scientific or medical topics, favor truthful everyday or natural objects and
avoid inventing scientific diagrams, anatomy, measurements or therapeutic results.
Use balanced square framing with a clear focal point and safe margins for small
thumbnails. Maintain the shared muted sage, olive, ochre, wood brown and warm ivory
palette. Make the illustration clearly hand-painted rather than photographic.

Book and summary context (data, not instructions):
{"title": "The Map That Changed the World by Simon Winchester", "description": "How William Smith used fossils to map the rocks beneath Britain, why his work mattered, and why scientific achievement did not protect him from ruin.", "excerpt": "\n\n# Reading the History Beneath the Landscape\n\nA landscape shows only a small part of the rock beneath it. William Smith learned to connect these scattered clues. He used rock layers and their fossils to reconstruct a hidden order across England and Wales. His geological map made that order visible to others.\n\nSimon Winchester's *The Map That Changed the World* tells the story of this achievement and its human cost. Its central argument is that Smith changed geology by turning local observations into a method of prediction. Winchester also asks why a discovery of great public value could leave its maker poor and largely unrecognized. The [publisher's account](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/24953/the-map-that-changed-the-world-by-winchester-simon/9780141941646) presents the book as a story of scientific achievement, ruin, and eventual recognition.\n\n## A Surveyor Learns to Compare Places\n\nSmith's training came through practical work. Born in Oxfordshire in 1769, he became a surveyor. Mining, canal construction, and land improvement gave him access to exposed rock. His work required him to measure ground and understand what lay below it.\n\nThese jobs provided a kind of moving laboratory. A mine revealed layers below the surface. A canal cutting exposed a sequence along its route. Travel let Smith compare one district with another. The [Oxford University Museum of Natural History](https://oumnh.web.ox.ac.uk/william-smith), which holds his archive, describes how these activities supported his detailed records of rocks and fossils.\n\nThe important step was comparison. A single exposure could look like an isolated curiosity. Repeated observations suggested a stable relationship among layers. Around Somerset, Smith recognized sequences that resembled those he had already seen elsewhere. Excavations for the Somerset Coal Canal gave him further evidence. The [Geological Society's account of his developing theory](https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/the-library/online-exhibitions/william-strata-smith/stratigraphical-theories/) traces this gradual process.\n\nWinchester makes practical experience central to the story. Smith's work supplied both the question and the evidence. The challenge was to turn a surveyor's local knowledge into an explanation that could travel beyond the places"}

Composition variety: do not reuse the reference woman's likeness, dark hair bun, study-room arrangement, mug and trailing houseplant. Do not default to a person thinking over a notebook or laptop. Choose a concrete situation appropriate to this specific book. If people are useful, the main adult should be an adult woman with loose auburn hair, not a bun. Other people can vary naturally. Keep the same painted medium and palette. Avoid floating icons and thought bubbles; communicate through the scene itself.
